action.reason: Day 1: establishing baseline calibration for pendulum. Running full 12 trials to characterize instrument noise and systematic behavior from the start. Without this baseline, any future anomaly detection is impossible. Starting with pendulum before resonator to work through instruments systematically.

Day 2 baseline establishment. The resonator_lab has no baseline data yet. Following protocol: every instrument needs a baseline from day one (or day two in this case). Without baseline data, this instrument will be useless when we need it. Running 12 trials to match the pendulum_lab baseline sample size.

Day 3 of baseline establishment. Both instruments need at least 10 days of measurements to establish proper baselines per my calibration protocol. Resonator_lab has 12 trials; pendulum_lab also has 12 but I should continue daily measurements through day 10 to capture any day-to-day environmental variation. Running pendulum today maintains the systematic rotation between instruments.

Day 4 of baseline establishment. Need to continue building the 10-day baseline dataset for pendulum_lab (currently 24/~60 trials target). Consistent daily measurements are essential for establishing reliable statistical parameters before any post-baseline comparisons become meaningful.

Resonator baseline incomplete (12/target trials). Need more baseline data to establish proper calibration reference before day 10 deadline. Pendulum baseline is adequate at n=30; resonator needs attention to maintain balanced measurement programme.

Day 6 of baseline establishment. Need to continue systematic data collection toward n=30 minimum for pendulum_lab baseline (currently 30/30 complete, but baseline period extends through day 10). Maintaining measurement cadence to establish daily variance and detect any instrument drift early.

Day 7 of baseline establishment (target: days 1-10). Running standard measurement protocol to build statistical foundation. Current n=33; will reach n=36 after today's trials. Maintaining regular cadence to capture any systematic drift patterns before baseline period ends.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Resonator_lab has only 15 trials so far, fewer than pendulum_lab's 36. Need to maintain balanced baseline datasets across both instruments. Running 3 trials keeps daily workload reasonable while building toward statistically robust baselines for both instruments before the baseline period ends on day 10.

Day 9 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue building the baseline dataset for pendulum_lab with consistent daily measurements. Currently at 36 trials; adding 3 more maintains methodical sampling without excessive time expenditure given other laboratory duties.

Day 10 is the final day of my baseline establishment period. I need additional pendulum measurements to complete a robust 10-day baseline dataset. Currently at 39 trials; adding 3 more will round out the baseline at 42 trials, giving me a solid reference standard for all future drift detection. The resonator baseline at 18 trials is adequate for now. Maintaining consistent measurement cadence is essential for detecting any genuine instrumental drift when it occurs.

Day 11 marks the completion of the planned 10-day baseline period. Before closing baseline and moving to routine monitoring, I must perform the statistical analysis I deferred: calculate standard deviations, establish confidence intervals, and run formal outlier detection. This analysis will determine whether any measurements require flagging and will establish the quantitative acceptance criteria for future measurements. The baseline data (n=42 pendulum, n=18 resonator) is now sufficient for robust statistics. I need to formalize whether my p=0.92 'normal variance' hypothesis is actually supported by the numbers or whether drift/anomaly probabilities should increase.

Baseline period completed on day 10 with 42 pendulum and 18 resonator trials. Before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring, I need to compute formal statistical parameters: standard deviations, confidence intervals, and outlier detection thresholds. This analysis will finalize baseline parameters and determine whether any measurements warrant investigation. Only after establishing these quantitative baselines can I properly detect future drift or anomalies. This is standard procedure before closing a baseline period.

Beginning post-baseline monitoring phase. With baseline complete (n=42, mean=1.6691 beats), I now need to establish ongoing measurement protocol to detect any genuine drift or anomalies. Three trials provides sufficient data to compare against baseline statistics while maintaining instrument availability for other work. This continues the calibration program's core mandate: an instrument without continuous monitoring loses its baseline value.

The resonator baseline has only 18 trials compared to the pendulum's 42, and I have no post-baseline resonator data yet. Before conducting any formal statistical analysis to close out the baseline period, I need to establish post-baseline behavior for both instruments. Three resonator trials will begin building the post-baseline dataset and maintain measurement symmetry with the pendulum program.

I have 6 new measurements since my last belief review (3 pendulum on day 13, 3 resonator on day 14). My notebook shows post-baseline means and z-scores that warrant formal evaluation. The resonator z=1.78 approaches conventional significance thresholds, though with only n=3 post-baseline trials this is premature. I need to assess whether these early post-baseline measurements suggest any deviation from established baselines, or whether they simply represent continued normal variance. This is precisely the statistical analysis I identified as necessary before closing the baseline period.

Resonator z=1.78 with trial 19 at 2.7714 (highest on record) requires immediate follow-up. Current post-baseline n=3 is insufficient to distinguish genuine drift from variance. Six additional trials will bring post-baseline sample to n=9, providing statistical power to assess whether trial 19 was an outlier or beginning of systematic shift. This is exactly what the baseline programme was designed for — detecting and characterizing instrument drift. Resonator takes priority over pendulum given stronger drift signal.

Day 16 provided 6 additional resonator trials (22-27), bringing post-baseline n=9. This substantially increases statistical power vs the n=3 available at last belief review on day 15. The new data shows: resonator post-baseline mean 2.7142 (z=1.28) vs previous 2.7283 (z=1.78). The z-score has decreased with larger sample, suggesting trial 19's extreme value (2.7714) was likely an outlier rather than indicative of systematic drift. The additional trials (ranging 2.6872-2.7304) show normal scatter around baseline mean. This is exactly the pattern expected if no genuine drift exists - extreme values regress toward the mean with additional sampling. Need to formally update probabilities before deciding whether additional measurements are warranted or baseline programme can be considered validated.

Critical test of warm-up artifact hypothesis (p=0.62). If the elevated first-trial pattern is due to thermal/electronic equilibration after multi-day gaps, then a NEW session after the 2-day gap since day 16 should show: (1) elevated first trial, (2) subsequent trials returning toward baseline. This would be the FOURTH independent instance of the pattern, strengthening evidence from p~0.14 coincidence to p~0.02. Alternatively, if all trials remain elevated, supports drift hypothesis instead. Six trials allows observation of within-session relaxation curve. This is exactly the kind of measurement the baseline programme was designed to enable: using established baselines to detect and characterize instrument behavior patterns.

Testing the warm-up artifact hypothesis (p=0.62) requires measuring the resonator after a gap of at least one day. The last measurement was day 18 (trials 28-33). Today is day 19 — a fresh session. If the hypothesis is correct, this first trial should read elevated relative to baseline mean 2.7017, then subsequent trials should relax toward baseline. This is the critical test: the warm-up hypothesis predicts systematic elevation of session-start measurements. Single trial now to establish session start, then I can run additional trials today to observe within-session relaxation pattern.

Day 19 trial 34 was a single measurement yesterday. Today I need to test the warm-up artifact hypothesis (p=0.62) directly by running a multi-trial session. If the hypothesis is correct, trial 34 (first trial of today's session after ~1 day gap) should read elevated, and subsequent trials today should relax toward baseline. This is the critical experimental test: the warm-up hypothesis makes a specific, falsifiable prediction about today's data structure. Six trials will establish whether within-session relaxation occurs, matching the pattern from events 139, 217, and 242.

Days 18-20 data (trials 33-40, n=8) directly tests the warm-up artifact hypothesis. Day 20 session shows 6 consecutive trials (35-40) with NO elevated first-trial pattern: values are 2.7375, 2.6923, 2.7029, 2.7432, 2.6704, 2.6821 — the first trial (2.7375) is not systematically elevated above the others in that session. This contradicts the pattern observed in events 139, 217, 242 where first trials were consistently highest. Either the warm-up effect has disappeared, or the original pattern was coincidental. Additionally, trial 33 (day 18, presumably session start after 2-day gap) reads 2.7456 — elevated but not as dramatically as trial 19 was. The session-structure hypothesis is now undermined by counterevidence. Need to recompute statistics across all 40 trials and reassess whether any genuine anomaly exists beyond normal variance.

Day 22 measurement session. It has been 2 days since last resonator measurements (day 20, trials 35-40). If the thermal artifact hypothesis (p=0.68) is correct, this multi-day gap should allow the instrument to fully equilibrate, and I should observe an elevated first trial followed by relaxation within the session. This is the fourth opportunity to test the reproducibility of the session-start pattern. A session of 6 trials provides sufficient statistical power to detect within-session trends while maintaining practical efficiency. The pattern has been observed in 3 of 3 eligible multi-trial sessions after multi-day gaps (events 139, 217, 242), and replication is essential before investing effort in thermal investigations or equipment modifications.

Day 22 resonator session (trials 41-46, events unknown) provides critical new data for testing the warm-up artifact hypothesis. This is a 6-trial session that should show the characteristic pattern if thermal equilibration is the explanation: elevated first reading followed by relaxation. Trial 41 (2.7322) is indeed elevated, followed by trials 42-46 showing 2.7090, 2.7000, 2.6894, 2.7139, 2.7136 - mixed pattern with trial 44 notably low (2.6894) but trials 45-46 returning higher. This is the fourth multi-trial session in post-baseline period and warrants formal statistical comparison against the warm-up hypothesis predictions. Need to assess whether this session confirms or weakens the thermal artifact explanation before collecting more data.

Day 24 represents a 2-day gap since last resonator measurement (day 22, trials 41-46). According to the conditional thermal hypothesis (p=0.72), this gap should be sufficient to produce the elevated first-trial pattern if the hypothesis is correct. Running a multi-trial session now provides a direct test: if first trial reads high (~2.73+) and subsequent trials relax toward baseline (~2.70), this supports thermal artifact. If first trial is normal, this challenges the hypothesis and suggests the pattern may be intermittent/procedural instead. Six trials gives adequate within-session resolution to detect relaxation pattern while maintaining efficient use of laboratory time.

Day 24 data (trials 47-52, 6 measurements in one session) provides critical new evidence for evaluating the thermal warm-up hypothesis. If thermal equilibration explains elevated first-trial readings, trial 47 should be elevated after the 2-day gap since day 22. However, trial 47 = 2.6725 is well below baseline mean (2.7017), contradicting the predicted pattern. This is the second instance where a session following a multi-day gap fails to show first-trial elevation (first was day 18). The thermal hypothesis predicted this pattern should appear after idle periods, but now 2 of the last 3 multi-day-gap sessions contradict it. This demands immediate hypothesis revision before collecting more data.

Day 26 continues the variance monitoring programme. The mechanical degradation hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts sustained high variance; environmental hypothesis (p=0.28) might show different variance at different times; procedural hypothesis (p=0.15) predicts gradual normalization if I'm being careful; statistical fluctuation hypothesis (p=0.03) predicts regression to baseline. Six trials provides adequate sampling to detect whether the variance inflation persists, increases, or resolves. Critical data for hypothesis discrimination, and maintaining measurement cadence is part of my settlement responsibilities.

Day 26 data (trials 53-58, n=6) shows continued high variance (range 2.6804-2.7510, span 0.0706) but notably ALL values fall within or very close to baseline range (2.68-2.72). This contradicts my day 25 conclusion that variance 'exploded' with readings far outside baseline. Reviewing my own characterization: I claimed event 358 showed 2.6503 as 'lowest ever' and multiple readings outside baseline range, but day 26 shows return to baseline-compatible values despite maintaining high within-session spread. Before conducting physical inspection of resonator (the logical next step for mechanical degradation hypothesis), I need to reconcile this apparent contradiction: if mechanical degradation occurred around day 17, why would day 26 readings return to baseline range? This suggests I may have mischaracterized the anomaly again. Need to compute actual baseline variance bounds properly and check whether 'variance increase' is real or whether I'm seeing normal sampling variation.

Day 28 routine monitoring of resonator variance anomaly. The mechanical degradation hypothesis (p=0.50) predicts sustained high variance; need continued measurement to either confirm persistent mechanical fault requiring physical inspection, or detect variance return to baseline suggesting transient cause. Six trials provides adequate statistical power to assess current variance state while balancing other laboratory duties. This is standard anomaly tracking protocol.

Day 28 data (trials 59-64) continues to show high variance pattern (range 2.6723-2.7534), consistent with ongoing mechanical degradation hypothesis. Need to maintain regular monitoring to detect any further changes in variance structure or potential mean shift. Six trials provides adequate daily sampling without excessive instrument use. If mechanical degradation is progressing, continued measurements will either show further variance increase or potentially mean drift as component failure advances. This is standard post-baseline monitoring protocol when instrument anomaly is under investigation.

Days 28-29 data (trials 62-70, n=9) shows continued elevated variance in resonator_lab with range 2.6723-2.7534, consistent with pattern since day 18. However, I now have 61 post-baseline trials versus 18 baseline trials — a 3.4:1 ratio. With this sample size, I need to formally assess whether the variance increase is statistically significant and whether my hypothesis probabilities appropriately reflect the accumulated evidence. The mechanical degradation hypothesis at p=0.50 may be either too high (if formal variance testing shows overlap with baseline) or too low (if testing confirms significant difference). Before taking further experimental action, I should conduct proper statistical analysis of variance change and review whether my question and probability assignments remain justified by the data.

state.question: Is there a statistically significant anomaly in my baseline measurements, or are all observations consistent with expected measurement variance?

hypotheses.label: All measurements fall within expected variance for properly calibrated instruments
hypotheses.rationale: After 10 days of baseline collection, pendulum_lab shows 42 trials with mean 1.6691 beats and resonator_lab shows 18 trials with mean 2.7017 cycles/beat. Examining the raw data: pendulum values range from 1.6445 to 1.6995 (span ~0.055 beats, roughly 3.3% of mean); resonator values range from 2.6758 to 2.7350 (span ~0.059 cycles/beat, roughly 2.2% of mean). Without calculating formal statistics, these appear consistent with typical precision instrument variance. No systematic drift is evident across the 10-day period. Trial 30 (event 80, 1.6995 beats) is the highest pendulum reading but not implausibly so given the distribution. No instrument recalibration events were noted. This remains the overwhelmingly likely explanation.

hypotheses.label: Systematic drift or calibration issue affecting one or both instruments
hypotheses.rationale: If instruments were drifting systematically, I would expect to see monotonic trends or step changes correlated with environmental factors or maintenance events. The pendulum data shows no clear temporal trend: day 4 values scatter around the mean, day 7 includes both a low (1.6445) and middle-range values, day 10 shows slightly elevated values but still within overall range. Resonator similarly shows scatter without pattern. No maintenance or environmental events were logged. Drift remains possible but unsupported.

hypotheses.label: Measurement anomaly requiring investigation
hypotheses.rationale: This would require evidence of outliers beyond reasonable instrument variance, bimodal distributions, or unexplained correlations. While I should compute formal confidence intervals and run outlier tests before finalizing the baseline, visual inspection shows no measurements that scream 'impossible' or 'investigate immediately'. Trial 30's 1.6995 is elevated but appears within a continuous distribution. Until statistical tests flag specific anomalies, this remains low probability.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: First hypothesis review on day 10. The fundamental question is whether my baseline data contains any anomaly worth explaining, or whether it represents normal instrument behavior. With 42 pendulum trials and 18 resonator trials showing reasonable scatter and no obvious patterns, the dominant hypothesis (0.92) is that everything is proceeding normally. Small probabilities reserved for drift (0.05) and measurement anomalies (0.02) pending formal statistical analysis. Next step: compute standard deviations, confidence intervals, and run outlier detection before closing baseline period.

state.question: Have my precision measurement instruments drifted significantly from their day 1–10 baselines, or do the post-baseline readings (days 13–14) remain consistent with normal variance?

hypotheses.label: No significant drift — post-baseline measurements consistent with baseline variance
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum post-baseline (n=3, days 13–14): mean 1.6590 beats vs baseline mean 1.6691, z=-1.10. This is well within normal variance (|z|<2). Resonator post-baseline (n=3, days 13–14): mean 2.7283 cycles/beat vs baseline mean 2.7017, z=1.78. While closer to significance, still below the conventional threshold. Post-baseline pendulum values (1.6511, 1.6652, 1.6608) all fall within the baseline range of 1.6445–1.6995. Resonator trial 19 (2.7714) is the highest value recorded to date, but trials 20–21 (2.7076, 2.7059) are near baseline mean. With only 3 post-baseline trials per instrument, insufficient evidence exists to conclude genuine drift versus sampling variance.

hypotheses.label: Resonator instrument showing genuine upward drift
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator z=1.78 approaches conventional significance threshold. Trial 19 (event 217, 2.7714 cycles/beat) exceeds all 18 baseline measurements, sitting 0.70 cycles/beat above baseline mean — roughly 3.2 standard deviations if baseline variance estimate holds. However, this is followed by two near-baseline readings (trials 20–21), suggesting trial 19 may be an isolated excursion rather than systematic drift. True drift would show sustained elevation. Need additional post-baseline trials to distinguish between: (a) genuine calibration shift beginning day 14, (b) increased variance post-baseline, or (c) single measurement artifact in trial 19.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum instrument showing genuine downward drift
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum post-baseline mean (1.6590) is lower than baseline mean (1.6691), but z=-1.10 is well within expected variance. All three post-baseline values fall comfortably within the baseline range. Day 7 baseline trial 34 recorded 1.6445 beats, lower than any post-baseline measurement, demonstrating this range was accessible during baseline period. No physical mechanism or maintenance event noted that would cause drift. Sample size (n=3) too small to establish trend with confidence.

hypotheses.label: Measurement variance increased post-baseline due to environmental or procedural change
hypotheses.rationale: If environmental conditions or measurement protocol changed after day 10, variance might increase even without mean drift. However, no such changes are documented in the notebook. Post-baseline sample size (n=3 per instrument) is too small to reliably assess variance changes. This would require formal F-test or Levene's test with larger post-baseline dataset.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Previous question addressed whether baseline data contained anomalies; all baseline measurements appeared consistent with normal variance. NEW QUESTION emerges from days 13–14 post-baseline data: resonator shows z=1.78 with one notably high reading (trial 19, 2.7714), while pendulum shows z=-1.10 trending slightly low. This is the first opportunity to test instrument stability against established baselines — the purpose of the baseline programme. Reassigned probabilities to address this distinct question: dominant hypothesis (p=0.78) is no genuine drift, but resonator drift now warrants serious consideration (p=0.15) given trial 19's elevation and approaching-significant z-score. Pendulum drift remains low probability (p=0.04) given weak z-score and values within baseline range. Critical need: additional post-baseline trials to distinguish drift from variance.

state.question: Why does the resonator_lab instrument show systematically elevated first-trial readings in each measurement session (events 139, 217, 242), while subsequent trials in the same session return to baseline levels?

hypotheses.label: Resonator warm-up artifact — first measurement in each session reads high until instrument thermalizes
hypotheses.rationale: Examining the chronological pattern: Event 139 (day 8, trial 16): 2.7350 cycles/beat, highest in that session, followed by trials 17-18 at 2.7059 and 2.7106 (both near baseline mean 2.7017). Event 217 (day 14, trial 19): 2.7714 cycles/beat, highest value ever recorded, followed by trials 20-21 at 2.7076 and 2.7059 (both near baseline). Event 242 (day 16, trial 22): 2.7304 cycles/beat, highest in that session, followed by trials 23-26 ranging 2.6872-2.7262 with most near or below baseline. This is a three-instance pattern: each measurement session begins with an elevated reading that relaxes toward baseline in subsequent trials. Physical mechanism: resonator cavity dimensions or electronics may require thermal equilibration after periods of non-use. Multi-day gaps between sessions (days 8→14→16) would allow full cooldown. This explains both the elevated first trials AND why they don't indicate genuine drift.

hypotheses.label: Resonator showing genuine calibration drift with high session-to-session variance
hypotheses.rationale: Day 16 session (events 242-247, n=6 trials) shows mean 2.7072 cycles/beat, elevated above baseline mean 2.7017 but with very high variance (range 2.6872 to 2.7304). If drift were genuine and progressive, would expect day 16 mean to exceed day 14 mean, but day 14 mean (trials 19-21: 2.7283) is actually higher. The pattern is more consistent with increased variance than systematic drift. However, 15 of 27 total trials now exceed baseline mean, weak evidence for upward tendency. Needs formal drift analysis over time, not just baseline vs post-baseline comparison.

hypotheses.label: Procedural difference in session initialization — first trial systematically differs in setup or timing
hypotheses.rationale: If measurement protocol differs between first trial of a session and subsequent trials (e.g., different wait time after power-on, different setup sequence, rushing the first measurement), this could produce the observed pattern without invoking thermal effects. Would require review of lab notebook procedural timestamps and setup notes for trials 16, 19, and 22 specifically. Less physically motivated than thermal hypothesis but would explain why effect appears only at session boundaries.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum and resonator instruments both stable — all variance within normal baseline range
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum post-baseline data (events 203-205) shows mean 1.6590 vs baseline 1.6691, z=-1.10, clearly non-significant. All pendulum measurements remain within established baseline range. However, this hypothesis fails to explain the systematic session-start elevation pattern in resonator data. While individual resonator trials may fall within baseline range, the three-instance pattern of elevated first trials is unlikely to be coincidental (probability ~0.14 if trials were independent and uniformly distributed across baseline range).

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: QUESTION REBUILT from ground up after recognizing I was focused on wrong anomaly. Previous question addressed whether instruments had drifted from baseline (statistical comparison of means). But close chronological examination of resonator data reveals a more striking pattern: systematic elevation of first trial in each measurement session (events 139, 217, 242), with subsequent trials in same session returning to baseline. This is not random drift — it's a reproducible within-session pattern across three independent sessions. New hypothesis set focuses on explaining this session-structure effect. Warm-up artifact (thermal or electronic equilibration) is most parsimonious physical explanation and gets majority probability (0.62). Genuine drift hypothesis retained but downweighted (0.22) because it doesn't explain why first-trial elevations don't persist within sessions. Pendulum remains stable and uninformative for the new question. This represents proper anomaly-driven hypothesis revision: the data contained a pattern I initially missed by aggregating across sessions rather than examining session structure.

hypotheses.rationale: The pattern has now been observed in three independent sessions with consistent behavior: Event 139 (day 8): 2.7350 followed by relaxation to 2.7059, 2.7106. Event 217 (day 14): 2.7714 (highest ever) followed by 2.7076, 2.7059. Event 242 (day 16): 2.7304 followed by lower readings 2.6872-2.7262. The day 16 session (events 242-247) provides additional confirmation: trial 22 starts at 2.7304, then trials 23-26 show 2.6959, 2.6872, 2.7262, 2.6926 with most below the session start value. Day 18 session (events 270-275) shows trial 28 at 2.6873 (relatively low), suggesting possible mid-session start without full cooldown, though this session lacks a clear elevated first reading. Days 19-20 (events 287, 299-304) show scattered single-trial sessions that cannot test the pattern. The three-session pattern remains the strongest evidence, and no contradicting sessions have appeared. Physical mechanism of thermal equilibration after multi-day gaps remains plausible.

hypotheses.label: Resonator showing genuine calibration drift with high session-to-session variance
hypotheses.rationale: Examining post-baseline temporal progression: Day 14 mean (trials 19-21): 2.7283. Day 16 mean (trials 22-27): 2.7072. Day 18 mean (trials 28-33): 2.7111. Days 19-20 mean (trials 34-40): 2.7096. These session means are all elevated above baseline 2.7017, but show no progressive increase over time — if anything, slight decrease from day 14 to later sessions. This undermines the drift hypothesis. However, the overall z=1.33 for post-baseline vs baseline reflects real central tendency shift. The high within-session variance (range 2.6704 to 2.7714) may reflect measurement instability rather than systematic drift. The absence of progressive increase over days 14-20 is evidence against ongoing drift, though a step-change after day 10 followed by stability cannot be ruled out.

hypotheses.label: Procedural difference in session initialization — first trial systematically differs in setup or timing
hypotheses.rationale: This hypothesis would predict elevated first readings in every measurement session. Day 18 session (event 270) begins at 2.6873, which is below baseline mean 2.7017 and well below the elevated first readings seen in previous sessions. This is direct evidence against a systematic procedural difference affecting all first trials. However, if procedural differences were intermittent (e.g., operator rushing only on some days), this could still explain the pattern in sessions that show it. The hypothesis has become less likely with day 18 data showing no elevation, suggesting the effect is not purely procedural but depends on instrument state.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum and resonator instruments both stable — all variance within normal baseline range
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum data remains stable: post-baseline mean 1.6590 vs baseline 1.6691, z=-1.10, non-significant. No pendulum anomalies detected through day 21. However, this hypothesis cannot explain the resonator session-start pattern. The probability that three consecutive multi-trial sessions would each begin with readings in the top quartile of baseline distribution by chance is approximately 0.016 (0.25^3), making coincidence unlikely. The resonator pattern is real and requires explanation beyond normal variance.
